deep.reconstruction:
Folio 13v carries no original writing. Everything visible is mirror-image bleed-through of the ink on the other side of the leaf. The layout and recognisable shapes match the transcription given as the 'previous page' (folio 13 recto) exactly. Reading the image right to left, as mirrored:

- At top right: the Poisson equation Δv = 4πρ.
- The line 'v, ∂v/∂n'.
- The definitions x' = ∂v/∂x, ... and dv = x'dx + y'dy + z'dz.
- The block of divergence and curl conditions (∂x'/∂y − ∂y'/∂x = 0, etc.).
- The decay conditions r∞² x' = 0, etc.
- The one-dimensional wave equations c²η_xx = η_tt and the d'Alembert form η = f(x+ct) + f(x−ct).
- The three-dimensional wave equations.
- The split x' = x1' + x2', ... into two parts. Part 1 is divergence-free and curl-free; part 2 has the divergence-type condition ∂x2'/∂x ... = 0 and satisfies x2''' = c²Δx2'.
- Near the bottom: the remark that the wave operator applied to (∂x'/∂y − ∂y'/∂x) gives 0. This comes from differentiating the component wave equations, x''' and y''', in y and x and subtracting.
- In the upper middle: v = ∫_0^s (∂v/∂s) ds, the labels x1' y1' z1' and x2' y2' z2', and η_tt = c·Δε.
- The folio number '13' is also visible, mirrored, near the left edge.

The mathematical content, all belonging to 13r, is a sketch for an aether or elasticity theory of light. It splits a displacement or velocity field into a curl-free (longitudinal) part and a divergence-free (transverse) part. It notes that each Cartesian component satisfies the wave equation c²Δu = u_tt, and that because the wave operator has constant coefficients it commutes with div and curl, so these combinations satisfy the same equation. Folio 13v contributes nothing beyond that.
errors: No errors can be assessed on 13v itself: it contains no original derivation, only show-through from 13r.

One slip belongs to 13r, not this page: there the d'Alembert solution is written η = f(x+ct) + f(x−ct) with the same function f twice instead of two arbitrary functions. That is a special symmetric case, not the general solution.

results.what: No independent result on this page. The bleed-through reproduces 13r: splitting a vector field into curl-free and divergence-free parts, each obeying the wave equation.
results.modern_name: Helmholtz decomposition; longitudinal and transverse wave decomposition in linear elasticity
results.usually_credited_to: Stokes (1849) and Helmholtz (1858); the elastic aether wave equations go back to Cauchy, Poisson and Green (1820s–1830s)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is blank apart from mirror-image show-through of folio 13r. Even the content of 13r is routine mid-19th-century aether and elasticity material.

checkable.sympy: from sympy import *; x,y,z,t,c=symbols('x y z t c'); X=Function('X')(x,y,z,t); Y=Function('Y')(x,y,z,t); W=lambda f: c**2*(diff(f,x,2)+diff(f,y,2)+diff(f,z,2))-diff(f,t,2); simplify(W(diff(X,y)-diff(Y,x)) - (diff(W(X),y)-diff(W(Y),x)))==0
checkable.asserts: The wave operator commutes with the curl component ∂X/∂y − ∂Y/∂x. This is the step visible in the bleed-through and belonging to 13r.

checkable.sympy: from sympy import *; x,t,c=symbols('x t c'); f=Function('f'); g=Function('g'); eta=f(x+c*t)+g(x-c*t); simplify(c**2*diff(eta,x,2)-diff(eta,t,2))==0
checkable.asserts: The d'Alembert form solves c²η_xx = η_tt, as on 13r. The general solution needs two independent functions f and g.
